title: Kernel fallback footprint scan: quantized kernels vs safe-contingency memory
content:
Purpose:
This is an experimental scan to understand the memory footprint and quality/latency tradeoffs when the runtime switches from an optimized low-precision kernel to a conservative 'safe' kernel under pressure (OOM, tiling limits, alignment failures). Unlike our throughput sweeps this focuses on the edge cases that trigger fallbacks and the downstream cost (latency spike, token-cost change, output drift).

Motivation / problem statement:
- Customers observe rare but high-severity tail latency events when serving quantized models. Root cause is often a kernel fallback that happens mid-request (tiling mismatch, KV-cache allocation, or kernel heuristic misprediction).
- We need an empirical map: what conditions (seq len, batch mix, kv-cache hits, transient memory pressure) cause specific kernels (INT8/AWQ/GPQT/FP8 variants) to fall back, and what is the measurable penalty in latency, throughput, and quality.

Scope and constraints:
- Hardware: single-node tests on p4d.24xlarge-equivalent (A100-ish) and a lower-memory T4-equivalent for edge cases.
- Models: Llama-2-13B (FP16 baseline), Llama-2-7B-int8-gptq build, a 13B AWQ-v0.9 fold, and a custom FP8 experimental build we label fp8-ex0.
- Kernels: matmul_v1 (safe fp16 fallback), matmul_lowprec_v2 (INT8-AWQ tuned), kv_pack_fast, kv_pack_safe, attention_sparse_opt, attention_generic
- Workload mixes: single-stream long-context (seq=4096), mixed small/burst (seq 64/1024 alternating), multi-tenant multiplexed (8 tenants, varying seq lengths), cold-start warmup (first 100 requests after container spin-up).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency per-request, token throughput, memory high-water mark, kernel-switch events (type + timestamp), output-quality proxies (delta logprob vs fp16 baseline, instruction-following BLEU-like scaffold, and SQuAD EM on a fixed prompt set), and per-token token cost estimate.

Test harness and instrumentation:
- Agent harness: local runner (bench-runner-v2) that drives synthetic traffic and records per-request timeline. Each request records kernel trace (start/end per kernel), GPU memory footprint timeline (sampled 60Hz), and KV-cache allocation map.
- Fault injection: soft pressure injected by background eviction thread that allocates ephemeral GPU tensors to nudge kernel allocator into contingency paths. Also we vary batch_shape_timeout to simulate race conditions.
- Repro harness: each experiment is 60 minutes of steady-state traffic + 10 minute warmup. All experiments repeated 3x; median reported unless variability noted.

Parameter grid (representative):
- Model variant: fp16 (baseline), int8-gptq, awq-quant, fp8-ex0
- Batch shape: 1x64, 4x64, 1x1024, 2x1024, multiplex-8-mix
- Seq lengths: 64, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096
- KV cache policy: kv_pack_fast enabled/disabled
- Background pressure: none, 30% memory churn, 60% memory churn
- Kernel heuristic mode: optimistic (prefer low-precision), conservative (prefer safe)

Selected results (high level) — pithy summary:
- The most frequent fallback path observed: matmul_lowprec_v2 -> matmul_v1 (safe fp16) during tiling alignment failures at seq>1024 when kv_pack_fast tried to pin a tiled KV region. On p4-equivalent this led to a mean p95 latency multiplier of ~3.2x for affected requests.
- AWQ builds had fewer math mismatches but more frequent kv_pack_safe fallbacks when batch_shape varied rapidly (multiplex workloads).
- FP8-ex0 produced slightly better token-cost in steady-state (token cost -6% vs int8) but had more brittle kernel dispatch (2–3x more fallback events under 60% churn).
- GPTQ int8 showed the best quality-preservation (delta logprob median < 0.02) but incurred a measurable throughput regression under multiplexed small batches due to less efficient vector-lane packing in matmul_lowprec_v2.
- Cold-starts: first 20 requests after container start show elevated fallback events due to allocator warmup; median latency for those requests was ~1.6x baseline even without injected pressure.

Representative microtrace (annotated):
- Request id 0x9f4: seq=2048, batch=1, model=int8-gptq
  00:0000 kernel dispatch -> matmul_lowprec_v2 (expected)
  00:0044 memory allocator -> alignment error on tiled slice
  00:0045 runtime: switch to matmul_v1 (safe)
  00:0047 kernel dispatch -> matmul_v1 end
  Observed latency: 700ms (baseline 230ms), delta logprob: 0.012

Quantified penalties (median across repeats):
- matmul fallback penalty: p95 +240–520ms on A100-equivalent for seq 1024–4096 (batch 1)
- kv_pack_safe fallback penalty: extra 30–120ms but lower memory high-water by ~150–300MB
- multiplexed small-batch penalty (due to packing mismatch): 15–40% throughput drop for int8 kernels vs fp16 kernel on p4-like hardware when batch_shape varies >20% per-second

Quality measurements (short prompt set, n=200 prompts):
- fp16 baseline: SQuAD EM 78.3, delta-logprob baseline set to 0.0
- int8-gptq: SQuAD EM 77.9 (drop 0.4), median delta logprob 0.018
- awq-0.9: SQuAD EM 77.4 (drop 0.9), delta logprob 0.032
- fp8-ex0: SQuAD EM 77.6 (drop 0.7), delta logprob 0.025
Notes: differences small on average but outlier prompts show >1.2 EM drop when fallback occurs mid-generation.

Hypotheses and root-cause notes:
- Tiling/packing heuristics are brittle at boundary sequence lengths where kernel tile width != model projection alignment. The allocator rarely returns precise slices required by matmul_lowprec_v2 which expects packed lanes.
- Multiplex workloads expose a race between packer and allocator; when batch_shape oscillates, packer tries to reuse non-contiguous memory and the allocator returns a fragment causing runtime to choose kv_pack_safe.
- FP8 kernels rely on a slightly tighter scratch-buffer estimate; when background churn increases the runtime conservatively picks safe kernels more often.

Immediate mitigations tested (working prototypes):
1) Opportunistic preflight check: before dispatching low-precision kernel, run a cheap preflight on a zeroed tile to validate alignment. If preflight fails, fallback to alternate packing strategy instead of full kernel swap. Proto improved p95 by ~18% in one-off tests.
2) Soft stall-and-retry: when allocation alignment fails, attempt 1 retry with small delay and hint to allocator to produce contiguous region. Reduced fallback count by 42% under 30% churn, but added 8ms median latency overhead on successful paths.
3) Conservative cold-start warmup: allocate and free a set of canonical tile shapes on container startup to stabilize allocator behavior. Eliminated 60% of cold-start fallbacks in the run.

Longer-term engineering directions:
- Kernel adaptivity: extend the kernel selector to consider memory-fragmentation heuristics and to prefer kernels that have lower fallback risk given current allocation fragmentation score.
- Packed-allocator redesign: explore a tag-based allocator that can provide contiguous tile guarantees for the top-k hot tile shapes (performance vs memory fragmentation tradeoff).
- Observability: emit a concise fallback event dimension in trace logs with tags (reason=alignment|OOM|tiling_mismatch, kernel_from, kernel_to, seq_len, batch_shape, mem_hwm). Make this parsable by our rollout dashboards so we can correlate increase in fallback rate with customer traffic patterns.

Open action items / tickets:
- ENG-PR-515: implement opportunistic preflight check and run full sweep across all kernel builds (owner: Marcus)
- ENG-PR-519: add fallback event telemetry and dashboard (owner: Elena)
- ENG-PR-522: reproduce T4-equivalent brittle failure and collect microtraces for allocator (owner: Samir)

Questions / items for review:
- Is the warmup allocation approach acceptable for Dedicated environments where memory reservation matters? We trade small steady-state overhead for lower tail events.
- Should we default to a single retry attempt on allocation failure, or gate this behind a runtime flag per-customer (default on for hosted)?
- Priority: do we prefer a kernel-level fix (hard) or allocator change (riskier but general)?

Appendix: quick checklist to reproduce locally
- checkout: git@github.com:redwood-inference/serveflow.git @ pr/4123
- bench-runner: bench-runner-v2 --model l2-13b-int8-gptq --seq 1024 --batch 1 --duration 3600 --trace-fallbacks --mem-churn 0.6
- env: USE_ALLOCA_HINT=1 KERNEL_HEURISTIC=optimistic

Raw artifacts: stored in gcs://redwood-serveflow-qa/fallback-scan/may2026/ (traces, raw profiles, perf counters)

Notes to self: write a short Slack explainer for customer-facing SREs that summarizes this: "rare kernel fallbacks cause large p95 spikes; immediate mitigations reduce events by ~40–60% on tests; longer-term plan to improve selector and allocator."

-- Aisha
